[Video 13  [](https://www.instagram.com/byfoodiegal) byfoodiegal 7.9M 🇰🇷 MUST VISIT MUSEUM IN SEOUL 📍National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea I always make it a mission to visit an art gallery when I travel. The gallery is free to enter, however some of the exhibits here costs. This particular exhibit is 2000/$2.30 or free for students and under 25, and you need to show ID. This performance exhibit “Hyundai Motor Series 2022: Choe U-Ram – Little Ark” is the epitome of contemporary and modern art, pushing the boundaries of the once oil-on-canvas beau ideal, whilst compelling and challenging one’s thoughts and belief systems. Round Table is the clever mechanically engineered artwork featured in this reel and the first in the exhibit. It is of 18 headless straw figures competing to occupy the single head that is rotating on the table, unbeknownst to this unachievable mission. Constantly fighting for the pursuit of what? a head? intelligence? survival? money? capitalism? [Video 16  [](https://www.instagram.com/mindonmymonet) mindonmymonet 19.9K ✨We went to check out @southlondongallery’s latest immersive exhibition. This time in the form of @leonardodrewstudio’s explosive Ubiquity II. 💥 This is Drew’s first solo exhibition in a London institution (and what a brilliant one it is!). The new site-specific work takes the form of two sculptural mountains that seem to spill throughout the gallery, while pushing the boundaries of abstraction. As a child Drew was initially inspired by the legendary comics of DC and Marvel, before turning to abstraction after seeing a reproduction of a painting by Jackson Pollock at his local library. This very much feels like a merge of the two. Milo was so blown away that I couldn’t keep up with his enthusiasm. We spoke to a lovely invigilator who gave us further insight into the work and let us know it took around a month to complete (working at superhero speed). They also provided some of the same materials Drew used in the installation for Milo to feel and see up-close. It was such a lovely touch. Highly recommend a visit!](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DKSTRenNmZ4/?utm_source=popular_topic_grid)

World Expo+ Sarah Montani: Sferism - The New Art

## Welcome at


## Visit the exhibition of Augmented Reality Sculptures from Swiss Artist Sarah Montani
We are very honored to show our Art during the exhibition “Sferism - The New Art” at Moderna museet Stockholm.
AR art is three-dimensional, untouchable, odorless and weightless. This new art form is a phenomenon that cannot be adequately described with words: the fascination arises from experiencing it, from trying it out, and seeing it with one's own eyes. **It is the world's first art project to exhibit AR art in museums and make it available without application.**

## Have a look at some videos of the exhibition
Did you find our sculptures in the Museum? It would be a pleasure to see your fotos and videos. Just send them to [Sarah](mailto:sarah.montani@weblaw.ch) and get in touch with us.
To see the artworks, go to the Museum with your smartphone. Please ensure that location services are enabled on your smartphone. Go to this website and choose the name of the Museum to see the sculptures. AR art "appears" in front of and inside the museum and can be perceived through the lens of your camera. These **artworks are exclusively accessible in the world's largest museums during the World Expo+**, thanks to the latest technology (GEO AR), within a radius of 50 - 100 meters on museum grounds.
World Expo+ Sarah Montani: Sferism - The New Art

## Visit our other exhibitions in over 30 Museums worldwide


## Media


## "Experience the Unseen: Sarah Montani's Augmented Reality Sculptures Take Center Stage"
Swiss Artist Sarah Montani is proud to present a captivating exhibition featuring groundbreaking augmented reality (AR) sculptures.This extraordinary display of AR art showcases a new form of artistic expression that transcends traditional boundaries, captivating viewers and redefining the art experience. This exhibition was initiated by the artist. It is the dream of many artists to exhibit their art in a museum. However, to wait for an invitation is usually not purposeful, especially as an artist of the female gender: museums buy 90% of art from men.
AR art offers a three-dimensional, untouchable, odorless, and weightless encounter that cannot be adequately conveyed through words alone. The true fascination arises from the firsthand experience of trying it out and witnessing it with one's own eyes. This exhibition represents the world's first art project to showcase AR art in museums, making it accessible to visitors without the need for additional applications or downloads.
To explore these remarkable artworks, visitors are invited to the Museum, armed with their smartphones. It is essential to ensure that location services are enabled on the device. By accessing the designated website and selecting the name of the Museum, spectators can witness the AR art sculptures come to life, seamlessly blending into the physical environment. Through the lens of a smartphone camera, these captivating artworks "appear" in front of and inside the museum, offering an immersive and interactive experience. This exclusive access to AR art is made possible by the latest technology (GEO AR), enabling viewing within a radius of 50-100 meters on the museum grounds.
Sarah Montani is aiming to revolutionize the way audiences engage with art in museums. By embracing cutting-edge technology and pushing the boundaries of creativity, this display provides a truly unique and unforgettable encounter for art enthusiasts of all ages.
Visitors are encouraged to seize this opportunity to experience the wonders of AR sculptures firsthand. The exhibition will transport viewers to a realm where art merges seamlessly with the digital world, eliciting a sense of wonder and awe.
For more information and to stay updated on the exhibition, please visit the official website at sarahmontani.com.

## "Experience the Unseen: Sarah Montani's Augmented Reality Sculptures Take Center Stage"
About Sarah Montani: Sarah Montani is a renowned Swiss artist celebrated for her innovative work in blending art and technology. With a passion for pushing artistic boundaries, Sarah's creations challenge conventional norms, providing viewers with unique and transformative experiences. Through her groundbreaking AR sculptures, she aims to redefine the art landscape and inspire audiences worldwide.

## Visit the exhibition of Augmented Reality Sculptures from Swiss Artist Sarah Montani
We are very honored to show our Art during the exhibition “Sferism - The New Art” at Moderna museet Stockholm.
AR art is three-dimensional, untouchable, odorless and weightless. This new art form is a phenomenon that cannot be adequately described with words: the fascination arises from experiencing it, from trying it out, and seeing it with one's own eyes. **It is the world's first art project to exhibit AR art in museums and make it available without application.**
texts.3:
## Have a look at some videos of the exhibition
Did you find our sculptures in the Museum? It would be a pleasure to see your fotos and videos. Just send them to [Sarah](mailto:sarah.montani@weblaw.ch) and get in touch with us.
To see the artworks, go to the Museum with your smartphone. Please ensure that location services are enabled on your smartphone. Go to this website and choose the name of the Museum to see the sculptures. AR art "appears" in front of and inside the museum and can be perceived through the lens of your camera. These **artworks are exclusively accessible in the world's largest museums during the World Expo+**, thanks to the latest technology (GEO AR), within a radius of 50 - 100 meters on museum grounds.

## "Experience the Unseen: Sarah Montani's Augmented Reality Sculptures Take Center Stage"
Swiss Artist Sarah Montani is proud to present a captivating exhibition featuring groundbreaking augmented reality (AR) sculptures.This extraordinary display of AR art showcases a new form of artistic expression that transcends traditional boundaries, captivating viewers and redefining the art experience. This exhibition was initiated by the artist. It is the dream of many artists to exhibit their art in a museum. However, to wait for an invitation is usually not purposeful, especially as an artist of the female gender: museums buy 90% of art from men.
AR art offers a three-dimensional, untouchable, odorless, and weightless encounter that cannot be adequately conveyed through words alone. The true fascination arises from the firsthand experience of trying it out and witnessing it with one's own eyes. This exhibition represents the world's first art project to showcase AR art in museums, making it accessible to visitors without the need for additional applications or downloads.
To explore these remarkable artworks, visitors are invited to the Museum, armed with their smartphones. It is essential to ensure that location services are enabled on the device. By accessing the designated website and selecting the name of the Museum, spectators can witness the AR art sculptures come to life, seamlessly blending into the physical environment. Through the lens of a smartphone camera, these captivating artworks "appear" in front of and inside the museum, offering an immersive and interactive experience. This exclusive access to AR art is made possible by the latest technology (GEO AR), enabling viewing within a radius of 50-100 meters on the museum grounds.
Sarah Montani is aiming to revolutionize the way audiences engage with art in museums. By embracing cutting-edge technology and pushing the boundaries of creativity, this display provides a truly unique and unforgettable encounter for art enthusiasts of all ages.
Visitors are encouraged to seize this opportunity to experience the wonders of AR sculptures firsthand. The exhibition will transport viewers to a realm where art merges seamlessly with the digital world, eliciting a sense of wonder and awe.
For more information and to stay updated on the exhibition, please visit the official website at sarahmontani.com.

# Hilma af Klint
The Ten Largest
22.9 2022–8.1 2023
Stockholm
Meet Hilma af Klint and her series of paintings “The Ten Largest”, when the works are once again on show in the museum in autumn 2022. This time the paintings will be exhibited together with a selection of the artist’s watercolours and a complete collection of hand-coloured photographs of “The Ten Largest” that has never previously been shown in its entirety.

Installation view from Hilma af Klint – The Ten Largest, 2022 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
It was autumn 1907 when the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) began the first canvas in a series that would come to be known as “The Ten Largest”. Working on these ten paintings over a period of just 40 days, the result she produced is one of the most monumental legacies of her artistic output. The series is part of a larger collection known as “Paintings for the Temple”, a mammoth project that the artist had embarked upon two years earlier after experiencing non-verbal cues from the spirit world. The challenge of understanding these messages and finding a visual expression for an invisible reality was to preoccupy Hilma af Klint throughout the rest of her life.
Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right context for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hundred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world.
Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 10, Ålderdomen, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Evolution and spirit worlds
The sheer size of “The Ten Largest” sets them apart from the artist’s other works. In a gigantic 3.28×2.40 metre format, Hilma af Klint celebrates the four ages of humanity: Childhood, Youth, Adulthood and Old Age.
A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.
This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.

# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Close collaboration with The Hilma af Klint Foundation
Thanks to the close collaboration between Moderna Museet and The Hilma af Klint Foundation, in autumn 2022 visitors to the Museum can renew their acquaintance with “The Ten Largest” by Hilma af Klint, showing in Stockholm for the first time since 2013.
The exhibition also includes a selection of watercolours and a collection of hand-coloured photographs that has never previously been on public display in its entirety.

268 Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 – 21 October 1944) was a Swedish artist and mystic whose paintings are considered to be among the first major abstract works in Western art history. A considerable body of her work predates the first purely abstract compositions by Kandinsky, Malevich, and Mondrian. She belonged to a group called “The Five”, a circle of women inspired by Theosophy who shared a belief in the importance of trying to contact the “High Masters”, often through séances. Her paintings, which sometimes resemble diagrams, were a visual representation of complex spiritual ideas. ( wikipedia) Images: from different sources; music: The Sheltering Sky, Ryuichi Sakamoto. # Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
It was autumn 1907 when the Swedish artist Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) began the first canvas in a series that would come to be known as “The Ten Largest”. Working on these ten paintings over a period of just 40 days, the result she produced is one of the most monumental legacies of her artistic output. The series is part of a larger collection known as “Paintings for the Temple”, a mammoth project that the artist had embarked upon two years earlier after experiencing non-verbal cues from the spirit world. The challenge of understanding these messages and finding a visual expression for an invisible reality was to preoccupy Hilma af Klint throughout the rest of her life.
Throughout her life, Hilma af Klint sought the right context for her paintings and only showed them to a limited number of people while waiting for the world to become ready to receive their message. Today, more than a hundred years later, her work is acclaimed all over the world.
Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 10, Ålderdomen, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet
texts.4:
# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Evolution and spirit worlds
The sheer size of “The Ten Largest” sets them apart from the artist’s other works. In a gigantic 3.28×2.40 metre format, Hilma af Klint celebrates the four ages of humanity: Childhood, Youth, Adulthood and Old Age.
A central theme in “The Ten Largest”, as in the artist’s oeuvre as a whole, is the notion of evolution. Hilma af Klint, however, seems less concerned about evolution in terms of any physical development from one form of existence to another, and focuses instead on evolution on a spiritual plane.
This reflects an interest in spirituality and theosophy that she shared with many of her contemporaries.
texts.5:
# Hilma af Klint
## About the exhibition
### Close collaboration with The Hilma af Klint Foundation
Thanks to the close collaboration between Moderna Museet and The Hilma af Klint Foundation, in autumn 2022 visitors to the Museum can renew their acquaintance with “The Ten Largest” by Hilma af Klint, showing in Stockholm for the first time since 2013.
The exhibition also includes a selection of watercolours and a collection of hand-coloured photographs that has never previously been on public display in its entirety.

268 Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 – 21 October 1944) was a Swedish artist and mystic whose paintings are considered to be among the first major abstract works in Western art history. A considerable body of her work predates the first purely abstract compositions by Kandinsky, Malevich, and Mondrian. She belonged to a group called “The Five”, a circle of women inspired by Theosophy who shared a belief in the importance of trying to contact the “High Masters”, often through séances. Her paintings, which sometimes resemble diagrams, were a visual representation of complex spiritual ideas. ( wikipedia) Images: from different sources; music: The Sheltering Sky, Ryuichi Sakamoto. Encounter an artistic practice that crosses boundaries, where light and movement, abstraction and geometry come together – from delicate botanical drawings to mesmerising mirror mosaics and large-scale sculptures.
Together with curator Asrin Haidari, explore how Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s artistic practice was shaped between Tehran and New York, through encounters between Iranian visual and craft traditions and post-war artistic experimentation.
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian working in her studio in Tehran, Iran, 1975 © The Estate of Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian. Photographer unknown.

# Curatorial tour: Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian: Tehran/New York
## About the exhibition
### Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian: Teheran/New York
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian (1922–2019) is regarded as one of Iran’s most influential artists. Her work brings together Iranian visual traditions and post-war artistic experimentation in a visual language characterised by geometric abstraction, mirror mosaics and forms found in nature.
The exhibition “Tehran/New York” brings together around one hundred works dating from 1970 to 2015. It includes kaleidoscopic mirror mosaics, sculptural assemblages, collages, floral drawings, calligraphic works and the autobiographical “Heartache Boxes”.

Title: Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian's exhibition
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian (1922–2019) lived and worked in Tehran and New York at different times – two cities that came to shape her artistic career in different ways. Her art is characterised by geometric abstraction, reflective materials and the forms of the vegetable kingdom. All with influences from Iran’s rich visual culture and deep historical roots as well as post-war modernist movements. The exhibition presents the artist’s most famous works – the kaleidoscopic mirror mosaics – but also shows her breadth, including calligraphic drawings and collages.
Today, Shahroudy Farmanfarmaianis regarded as one of Iran’s most influential artists and holds an established place in global modernism and contemporary art history.
This is the first solo exhibition of her work in the Nordic countries. The exhibition is organised by Moderna Museet, Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, and Kunstmuseum Den Haag. From Moderna Museet, it will go on tour to Madrid and The Hague.
“Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s oeuvre makes visible connections and exchanges that have long fallen outside dominant narratives of modern art history. At the same time, her way of moving between materials, knowledge traditions and places resonates with concerns that are central to contemporary art today”, the exhibition’s curator Asrin Haidari says.

### Nearly one hundred works
The exhibitionincludes nearly 100 artworks, from the 1970s to works created by Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian in the 2010s. A key work that the audience encounters in the exhibition is _Third family_ (2011) – a series of mirror reliefs in which geometric shapes develop through repetition.
The mirror works are exhibited side by side with drawings, collages, textile works and the personal _Heartache boxes_, a kind of memory boxes. The exhibition shows how the artist allows geometric structure and mathematical precision to coexist with intuition and chance. Forms and ideas wander between materials and techniques, returning, changing and merging into new constellations.

### Opportunities and limitations
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s life and work were shaped by recurring departures and returns but also by exceptional opportunities. She was born in 1922 in Qazvin, Iran, into a wealthy and influential family. This gave her access to education, travel and contacts, while at the same time she faced a number of obstacles and limitations, both as a woman and as an Iranian artist. Political upheavals in Iran and the changing attitudes of the outside world towards the country had significant consequences for her opportunities to work and gain recognition as an artist.

### Tehran–New York, return
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian studied art at the University of Tehran before continuing her studies in New York in 1945. There she moved in the city’s avant-garde environments and established herself as a designer and illustrator. She meets Joan Mitchell, Robert Morris and Andy Warhol, among others, before their big breakthrough.
With impressions from the New York art scene and a degree in her bag, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian returned to Tehran in 1957, which was developing into a dynamic art metropolis. She became part of Iran’s growing art scene and already in 1958, she participated in both the first Tehran Biennial and the Venice Biennial. At the same time, she deepened her interest in Iran’s historical visual and craft traditions.
During her travels through Iran, she visited historic buildings, mosques and shrines, and studied the craft techniques and patterns she encountered there. Particularly significant was the visit to the Shah Cheragh shrine in Shiraz in 1966. The interiors, where walls and arches are covered in hand-cut geometric mirror pieces, made a deep impression and the experience became central to her continued work.

### Exile and return, and international breakthrough
When the revolution broke out in 1979, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian was in New York and could not return to Iran.
She lived in exile in New York for about 25 years. There, the conditions for her work were more constrained, and she turned to collages, drawings and smaller objects. Many of the ideas and forms she developed during this period would reappear in other materials much later.
In the early 2000s, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian returned permanently to Tehran and established her own studio. She once again gains access to materials, techniques and specialised craftsmanship, not least in the field of mirror mosaic. It becomes the prelude of one of the most productive periods in her artistic career. Well into her nineties, she continued to push the possibilities of geometry, materials and mirrors.
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian had her big international breakthrough with a retrospective exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York in 2015. Two years later, she donated 51 works from her private collection to the newly opened Monir Museum in Tehran, the first museum in Iran dedicated to an individual female artist.

Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian (1922–2019) lived and worked in Tehran and New York at different times – two cities that came to shape her artistic career in different ways. Her art is characterised by geometric abstraction, reflective materials and the forms of the vegetable kingdom. All with influences from Iran’s rich visual culture and deep historical roots as well as post-war modernist movements. The exhibition presents the artist’s most famous works – the kaleidoscopic mirror mosaics – but also shows her breadth, including calligraphic drawings and collages.
Today, Shahroudy Farmanfarmaianis regarded as one of Iran’s most influential artists and holds an established place in global modernism and contemporary art history.
This is the first solo exhibition of her work in the Nordic countries. The exhibition is organised by Moderna Museet, Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, and Kunstmuseum Den Haag. From Moderna Museet, it will go on tour to Madrid and The Hague.
“Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s oeuvre makes visible connections and exchanges that have long fallen outside dominant narratives of modern art history. At the same time, her way of moving between materials, knowledge traditions and places resonates with concerns that are central to contemporary art today”, the exhibition’s curator Asrin Haidari says.
texts.1:
### Nearly one hundred works
The exhibitionincludes nearly 100 artworks, from the 1970s to works created by Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian in the 2010s. A key work that the audience encounters in the exhibition is _Third family_ (2011) – a series of mirror reliefs in which geometric shapes develop through repetition.
The mirror works are exhibited side by side with drawings, collages, textile works and the personal _Heartache boxes_, a kind of memory boxes. The exhibition shows how the artist allows geometric structure and mathematical precision to coexist with intuition and chance. Forms and ideas wander between materials and techniques, returning, changing and merging into new constellations.
texts.2:
### Opportunities and limitations
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s life and work were shaped by recurring departures and returns but also by exceptional opportunities. She was born in 1922 in Qazvin, Iran, into a wealthy and influential family. This gave her access to education, travel and contacts, while at the same time she faced a number of obstacles and limitations, both as a woman and as an Iranian artist. Political upheavals in Iran and the changing attitudes of the outside world towards the country had significant consequences for her opportunities to work and gain recognition as an artist.
texts.3:
### Tehran–New York, return
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian studied art at the University of Tehran before continuing her studies in New York in 1945. There she moved in the city’s avant-garde environments and established herself as a designer and illustrator. She meets Joan Mitchell, Robert Morris and Andy Warhol, among others, before their big breakthrough.
With impressions from the New York art scene and a degree in her bag, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian returned to Tehran in 1957, which was developing into a dynamic art metropolis. She became part of Iran’s growing art scene and already in 1958, she participated in both the first Tehran Biennial and the Venice Biennial. At the same time, she deepened her interest in Iran’s historical visual and craft traditions.
During her travels through Iran, she visited historic buildings, mosques and shrines, and studied the craft techniques and patterns she encountered there. Particularly significant was the visit to the Shah Cheragh shrine in Shiraz in 1966. The interiors, where walls and arches are covered in hand-cut geometric mirror pieces, made a deep impression and the experience became central to her continued work.
texts.4:
### Exile and return, and international breakthrough
When the revolution broke out in 1979, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian was in New York and could not return to Iran.
She lived in exile in New York for about 25 years. There, the conditions for her work were more constrained, and she turned to collages, drawings and smaller objects. Many of the ideas and forms she developed during this period would reappear in other materials much later.
In the early 2000s, Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian returned permanently to Tehran and established her own studio. She once again gains access to materials, techniques and specialised craftsmanship, not least in the field of mirror mosaic. It becomes the prelude of one of the most productive periods in her artistic career. Well into her nineties, she continued to push the possibilities of geometry, materials and mirrors.
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian had her big international breakthrough with a retrospective exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum in New York in 2015. Two years later, she donated 51 works from her private collection to the newly opened Monir Museum in Tehran, the first museum in Iran dedicated to an individual female artist.

# Curatorial tour: Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian: Tehran/New York
## About the exhibition
### Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian: Teheran/New York
Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian (1922–2019) is regarded as one of Iran’s most influential artists. Her work brings together Iranian visual traditions and post-war artistic experimentation in a visual language characterised by geometric abstraction, mirror mosaics and forms found in nature.
The exhibition “Tehran/New York” brings together around one hundred works dating from 1970 to 2015. It includes kaleidoscopic mirror mosaics, sculptural assemblages, collages, floral drawings, calligraphic works and the autobiographical “Heartache Boxes”.

Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s major retrospective,_Tehran/New York_ opens at Moderna Museet, Stockholm. Curated by Asrin Haidari, the exhibition is organised in collaboration with Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, and Kunstmuseum Den Haag, Hague, and will travel to both venues in 2027.
Bringing together around one hundred works made between 1970 and 2015, the exhibition traces how Farmanfarmaian’s practice moved between two cities. Mirror mosaics and sculptural assemblages hang alongside collages, floral drawings, rugs, calligraphic works and her autobiographical ‘Heartache Boxes,’ as well as ‘Third Family’ (2011), one of her most expansive studies of the hexagon. Inspired by the ayeneh-kari of the Shah Cheragh shrine in Shiraz, she brought mirror mosaic out of architecture and into sculpture. She later rebuilt her practice through intimate works on paper during 25 years of exile in New York, then returned to Tehran in 2004 for one of the most productive periods of her career. "You become part of the art, and the art becomes part of you."
The exhibition is on view through 28 February 2027.
Visit the Moderna Museet website for more information.

Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian’s major retrospective,_Tehran/New York_ opens at Moderna Museet, Stockholm. Curated by Asrin Haidari, the exhibition is organised in collaboration with Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía, Madrid, and Kunstmuseum Den Haag, Hague, and will travel to both venues in 2027.
Bringing together around one hundred works made between 1970 and 2015, the exhibition traces how Farmanfarmaian’s practice moved between two cities. Mirror mosaics and sculptural assemblages hang alongside collages, floral drawings, rugs, calligraphic works and her autobiographical ‘Heartache Boxes,’ as well as ‘Third Family’ (2011), one of her most expansive studies of the hexagon. Inspired by the ayeneh-kari of the Shah Cheragh shrine in Shiraz, she brought mirror mosaic out of architecture and into sculpture. She later rebuilt her practice through intimate works on paper during 25 years of exile in New York, then returned to Tehran in 2004 for one of the most productive periods of her career. "You become part of the art, and the art becomes part of you."
The exhibition is on view through 28 February 2027.
Visit the Moderna Museet website for more information.

## Covid-19
In consultation with the other national museums, Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Malmö closed for the public on 22 March 2020 due to the covid pandemic. The museum adapted to the situation, and continued its efforts, to the extent that the restrictions allowed, to preserve the collection in the form of registering and conserving the art. New digital formats were launched to reach a large and broad public, and funding from private foundations were used to acquire Swedish contemporary art.
The exhibition “Giacometti – Face to Face” opened on 10 October, but the museum was forced to close again on 29 October. Malmö remained closed until 16 March 2022 and Stockholm until 25 March. During this closure, the museum continued to explore digital formats, such as live-broadcast “Sofa Tours”, workshops and “Create like…”
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”. The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.

## Covid-19
### A new manifesto
A comprehensive project involving the entire museum staff led to a manifesto that was announced by Gitte Ørskou in 2021. Moderna Museet should not distance itself from society but engage actively with the world, be inclusive and promote diversity, address a broader audience and embrace sustainable practices that take into account environmental and social impacts.
Just over a month after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, the museum in collaboration with Castello di Rivoli in Turin featured “A Letter from the Frontier” – 19 video works by 15 contemporary Ukrainian artists and artist groups, which could be viewed at the museum and on the Moderna Museet website.

## Covid-19
### Björn Lövin & Jeppe Hein
Throughout 2022, the museum paused all long-distance shipping of art. Among other things, this led to the exhibition “Björn Lövin – The Surrounding Reality”. None of Björn Lövin’s original so-called environments had been preserved since they were shown in the 1970s and 1980s, but three of them were reconstructed on site at the museum. Moderna Museet’s summer exhibition of Jeppe Hein was also produced on location, in interaction with visitors.
The year ended with a small exhibition of Hilma af Klint, attracting record visitor numbers.

## Covid-19
### New collection presentation
From 2023, Gitte Ørskou renewed the collection presentation through thematic exhibitions that made focused interventions across different periods and movements in 20th-century art. The first was “Sleepless Nights – From the 1980s in the Moderna Museet collection”. As part of the new presentation, artists such as Rashid Johnson and Maurizio Cattelan were also invited to select works from the collection.
Several artists were highlighted in solo exhibitions: Nan Goldin (2022), Laurie Anderson (2023), Lotte Laserstein (2023), Monica Sjöö (2023) and Britta Marakatt-Labba (2025).
At the end of 2025, Carsten Höller’s slides, “Stockholm Slides”, were installed on the museum’s façade, coinciding with the opening of a major Picasso exhibition featuring late works.

## Covid-19
### 2026 – Towards a new organisational structure
Moderna Museet is entering a new era of organisational change. In 2024, the Government decided to incorporate Statens konstråd and ArkDes into Moderna Museet. As of 1 January 2026, both institutions became part of the Moderna Museet government organisation.
Gitte Ørskou will leave her post in August 2026, and in September Tone Hansen will take up the position of Museum Director at Moderna Museet. Most recently, she served as Director of MUNCH in Oslo and previously led Henie Onstad Kunstsenter.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

What is the Moderna Museet Collection? A wonderful way to travel in time, art and ideas. Here, you will find some of the world’s finest art, modern and contemporary, Swedish and international, including key works by the most prominent artists of the 20th and 21st centuries.

# The Collection
## Which is your favorite artwork?
Moderna Museet has one of Europe’s finest collections of modern and contemporary art. It includes key works by Pablo Picasso, Ljubov Popova, Salvador Dalí, Meret Oppenheim, Robert Rauschenberg, Donald Judd and Irving Penn, along with works by contemporary practising artists.
The Moderna Museet collection comprises some 6,000 paintings, sculptures and installations, 25,000 watercolours, drawings and prints, 400 art videos and films, and 100,000 photographs (from the birth of photography to today).
Search the collection
Francis Picabia, Première rencontre/First Meeting, 1925 © Francis Picabia/ Bildupphovsrätt 2016

# The Collection
## About the collection


# The Collection
## The collection increases
Since the start in 1958, Moderna Museet has been known for its close relationship to artists – Marcel Duchamp, for instance, signed several of his works in Stockholm towards the end of his life, and Andy Warhol had his first solo museum exhibition in Europe at Moderna Museet in 1968.
Thanks to focused collecting initiatives, the Museum has successfully increased the breadth and depth of its collection. Back in 1963, The Museum of Our Wishes was launched, transforming the Museum instantly into a leading European art institution; the government contributed SEK 5 million, for the acquisition of iconic works by Giacomo Balla, Francis Picabia, Kurt Schwitters, Giorgio de Chirico and many others.
A few decades ago, the exercise was repeated, but this time spotlighting women artists only – works by Louise Bourgeois, Dorothea Tanning, Judy Chicago, Susan Hiller and others were added to the collection.

# The Collection
## Swedish & Nordic art
Swedish and Nordic art naturally have a prominent place in the collection, since Moderna Museet is the central national museum for 20th and 21st century Swedish art.
Moderna Museet has the largest body of works by Öyvind Fahlström, Vera Nilsson, Siri Derkert, Dick Bengtsson and many other Swedish artists.

# The Collection
## Swedish & Nordic art
### Swedish Acquisitions 2021
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.

## Covid-19
In consultation with the other national museums, Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Malmö closed for the public on 22 March 2020 due to the covid pandemic. The museum adapted to the situation, and continued its efforts, to the extent that the restrictions allowed, to preserve the collection in the form of registering and conserving the art. New digital formats were launched to reach a large and broad public, and funding from private foundations were used to acquire Swedish contemporary art.
The exhibition “Giacometti – Face to Face” opened on 10 October, but the museum was forced to close again on 29 October. Malmö remained closed until 16 March 2022 and Stockholm until 25 March. During this closure, the museum continued to explore digital formats, such as live-broadcast “Sofa Tours”, workshops and “Create like…”
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”. The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.
texts.27:
## Covid-19
### A new manifesto
A comprehensive project involving the entire museum staff led to a manifesto that was announced by Gitte Ørskou in 2021. Moderna Museet should not distance itself from society but engage actively with the world, be inclusive and promote diversity, address a broader audience and embrace sustainable practices that take into account environmental and social impacts.
Just over a month after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, the museum in collaboration with Castello di Rivoli in Turin featured “A Letter from the Frontier” – 19 video works by 15 contemporary Ukrainian artists and artist groups, which could be viewed at the museum and on the Moderna Museet website.
texts.28:
## Covid-19
### Björn Lövin & Jeppe Hein
Throughout 2022, the museum paused all long-distance shipping of art. Among other things, this led to the exhibition “Björn Lövin – The Surrounding Reality”. None of Björn Lövin’s original so-called environments had been preserved since they were shown in the 1970s and 1980s, but three of them were reconstructed on site at the museum. Moderna Museet’s summer exhibition of Jeppe Hein was also produced on location, in interaction with visitors.
The year ended with a small exhibition of Hilma af Klint, attracting record visitor numbers.
texts.29:
## Covid-19
### New collection presentation
From 2023, Gitte Ørskou renewed the collection presentation through thematic exhibitions that made focused interventions across different periods and movements in 20th-century art. The first was “Sleepless Nights – From the 1980s in the Moderna Museet collection”. As part of the new presentation, artists such as Rashid Johnson and Maurizio Cattelan were also invited to select works from the collection.
Several artists were highlighted in solo exhibitions: Nan Goldin (2022), Laurie Anderson (2023), Lotte Laserstein (2023), Monica Sjöö (2023) and Britta Marakatt-Labba (2025).
At the end of 2025, Carsten Höller’s slides, “Stockholm Slides”, were installed on the museum’s façade, coinciding with the opening of a major Picasso exhibition featuring late works.
texts.30:
## Covid-19
### 2026 – Towards a new organisational structure
Moderna Museet is entering a new era of organisational change. In 2024, the Government decided to incorporate Statens konstråd and ArkDes into Moderna Museet. As of 1 January 2026, both institutions became part of the Moderna Museet government organisation.
Gitte Ørskou will leave her post in August 2026, and in September Tone Hansen will take up the position of Museum Director at Moderna Museet. Most recently, she served as Director of MUNCH in Oslo and previously led Henie Onstad Kunstsenter.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin
texts.4:
# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.
texts.5:
# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.

Moderna Museet has one of Europe’s finest collections of modern and contemporary art. It includes key works by Pablo Picasso, Ljubov Popova, Salvador Dalí, Meret Oppenheim, Robert Rauschenberg, Donald Judd and Irving Penn, along with works by contemporary practising artists.
The Moderna Museet collection comprises some 6,000 paintings, sculptures and installations, 25,000 watercolours, drawings and prints, 400 art videos and films, and 100,000 photographs (from the birth of photography to today).

texts.5:
# The Collection
## The collection increases
Since the start in 1958, Moderna Museet has been known for its close relationship to artists – Marcel Duchamp, for instance, signed several of his works in Stockholm towards the end of his life, and Andy Warhol had his first solo museum exhibition in Europe at Moderna Museet in 1968.
Thanks to focused collecting initiatives, the Museum has successfully increased the breadth and depth of its collection. Back in 1963, The Museum of Our Wishes was launched, transforming the Museum instantly into a leading European art institution; the government contributed SEK 5 million, for the acquisition of iconic works by Giacomo Balla, Francis Picabia, Kurt Schwitters, Giorgio de Chirico and many others.
A few decades ago, the exercise was repeated, but this time spotlighting women artists only – works by Louise Bourgeois, Dorothea Tanning, Judy Chicago, Susan Hiller and others were added to the collection.
texts.6:
# The Collection
## Swedish & Nordic art
Swedish and Nordic art naturally have a prominent place in the collection, since Moderna Museet is the central national museum for 20th and 21st century Swedish art.
Moderna Museet has the largest body of works by Öyvind Fahlström, Vera Nilsson, Siri Derkert, Dick Bengtsson and many other Swedish artists.

# The Collection
## Swedish & Nordic art
### Swedish Acquisitions 2021
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.

Stockholm
Nan Goldin is one of the most high-profile and controversial artists of our time. The retrospective “This Will Not End Well” is presented in six unique rooms. Experience her works as slideshows and films set to sound and music, where stories about love, intimacy, addiction, and loss take place on the screens.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

Hilma af Klint

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
10.4 2015
Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) was a pioneer of abstraction. As early as 1906 she had developed a rich, symbolic imagery that preceded the more broadly recognized emergence of abstract art. Since her retrospective at Moderna Museet in Stockholm in 2013, interest in the Swedish artist has increased all over the world. The exhibition "Hilma af Klint – Artist, Researcher, Medium"further expands our understanding of this groundbreaking artist and researcher.
Hilma af Klint, The Swan, No. 17, 1915 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
Hilma af Klint studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 where she focused on naturalistic landscape and portrait paintings. Like many of her contemporaries, af Klint also had a keen interest in invisible dimensions that exist beyond the visible world. When painting she was convinced that she was in contact with higher consciousness, which conveyed messages through her. Her major series, “The Paintings for the Temple”, became the crux of this artistic inquiry.
The exhibition centres on three aspects of Hilma af Klint’s life and interests – as artist, researcher and medium – that are key to revealing and understanding her art. With few exceptions, af Klint never exhibited her abstract works during her lifetime. Yet she left us with a radical body of work – unprecedented in its use of color, scale and composition – which she hoped future audiences might be better able to sense and decode.
Hilma af Klint made paintings for the future, and that future is now.

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Artist and medium
Like many of her contemporaries at the turn of the twentieth century, Hilma af Klint sought to expand her consciousness in order to gain a wider perspective on what we perceive as reality. Consciousness remains one of the deepest mysteries in our time, a subject eagerly explored in neurology, psychology, quantum physics and epigenetics. As part of her spiritual practice, af Klint meditated, adhered to a vegetarian diet, and studied Theosophy and Rosicrucianism. These two esoteric schools thought knowledge of a deeper spiritual reality could be achieved through focused attention on intuition, meditation, and other means of transcending normal human consciousness. Over a period of ten years, af Klint met weekly with four other women, known as De fem (“The Five”). They trained their capability to access or “channel” higher levels of consciousness through contact with spiritual guides known as De Höga(“The Masters”). Af Klint received a specific assignment, which she accepted, known as “The Paintings for the Temple”. She worked throughout her life to understand the deeper meaning embedded in these works.
> “The pictures were painted directly through me, without any preliminary drawings and with great force. I had no idea what the paintings were supposed to depict; nevertheless, I worked swiftly and surely, without changing a single brushstroke
The artist described how she painted the series as a medium, where shapes, colors and compositions came to her. Although af Klint perceived these works as flowing uninhibitedly through her guided hand, she very much applied herself and all her skills in the process: she worked methodically and sequentially in series, divided into thematically and formally focused groups exploring different aspects of cosmic and human evolution.

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## The paintings for the temple
Between 1906 and 1915, Hilma af Klint created “The Paintings for the Temple”. It comprises 193 paintings and drawings, divided into series and groups. Works produced between 1906 and 1908 are on view in the Turbine Hall; works from the second part of the series from 1912 to 1915 are on view in the upstairs galleries at Moderna Museet Malmö.
The overall theme of the series is to convey different aspects of human evolution, instigated by polarity. ”The Paintings for the Temple” also thematizes different stages of development that every human being goes through during life on earth. The temple in the title refers not only to a physical building, which af Klint imagined would house the work, but also to the body as a temple for the soul.

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Eros and The Seven-pointed Star+
Hilma af Klint, The Eros Series, No. 8, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
The exhibition opens with the joyful series dedicated to Eros, the Greek god of love, associated with fertility and desire. Full of life, these pink-hued works take up the theme of polarity between male and female as the driving force of evolution. These abstract works completely differ from the classic representation of Eros.
In the series “The Seven-Pointed Star”(1908), Hilma af Klint experimented with a greater economy of line, depicting spiraling energy expanding outwards and forming new centres. As is the case with most of af Klint’s work, there is no singular meaning. Seven is a sacred number in many cultures, associated with divine order, and also the eternal harmony of the universe. In Theosophy the star cluster, known as the Seven Stars or the Pleiades, transmits spiritual energy that eventually reaches the human plane.
The series ”Eros” and ”The Seven-pointed Star” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our art educator Ellen Arvidsson present one of the works from the series ”Eros”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Ten Largest+
Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 3, Ynglingaåldern, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet
Like many of the other series within “The Paintings for the Temple”, “The Ten Largest”seems somehow unfettered by limitations of place and time. Across ten canvases, swirling shapes in soft pastel colors rhythmically interact with cursive letters, forming a kind of visual poem. Petals, ovaries, flowers and spirals pulsate in constant sparks of creation. Hilma af Klint attributed this series to the exploration of the human life cycle, from childhood and youth to adulthood and old age. The artist created the ten works between November and December of 1907 on large sheets of paper later glued onto canvas. Given the unusual scale of the works, it is likely that af Klint painted each canvas, while it was lying flat on her studio floor.
The series ”The Ten Largest” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our art educator Mimmi Sjöö present one of the works from the series ”The Ten Largest”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Primordial Chaos+
Hlma af Klint, Primordial Chaos, No. 15, 1906 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
”Primordial Chaos” (1906–07) is devoted to the creation of the physical world. From the original unity a polarized world arose out of spirit, shown here as feminine (blue and the eyelet) and masculine (yellow and the hook), and also as W (material) and U (spirit). These works are full of spirals of energy and sparks of creation, of symbols of fertility and rebirth (sperm, snakes, crosses).
”Primorial Chaos” is displayed in the Turbine hall.

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Evolution+
Hilma af Klint, The Evolution, No. 7, 1908 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
The theme of the evolution of consciousness runs throughout “The Paintings for the Temple”. In the series ”Evolution” (1908), the process of development is shown through the interplay between polarities: male and female, light and darkness, good and evil. Compositionally these works strive to find a balance, in horizontal and vertical mirroring. Hilma af Klint’s exploration seems aligned with the theosophist notion of evolution as a spiritual process, extending beyond the biological perspective on human development that, with the publishing of Darwin’s ”The Evolution of the Species” fifty years earlier, had gained widespread notoriety. This series ends the first part of “The Paintings for the Temple”, as the commission was paused between 1908 and 1912.
The series ”Evololution” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our curator of learning Susanne Lindblad present one of the works from the series ”Evolution”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Swan and The Dove+
Hilma af Klint, The Dove, No. 1, 1915 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
When Hilma af Klint resumed her work on ”The Paintings for the Temple” in 1912, her abstraction became more geometric in nature, and Christian symbols became increasingly pronounced. When working, the artist was still in contact with higher planes of consciousness but was encouraged to interpret spiritual messages more freely.
Viewed in sequence, ”The Swan”(1914–15) has a distinct visual rhythm. Often a horizontal line breaks the canvases into two sections where opposite forces meet – light and dark, male and female, life and death. These poles unfold as a black and white swan. Eventually, figuration gives way to abstraction in a fuller spectrum of color. In the final work in the series, the swan pair returns, unified at the centre, intertwined yet distinct and balanced as male and female poles.
The series ”The Swan” are displayed in the Upstairs Galleries.
Watch our art educator Sannie Johansen present one of the works from the series ”The Swan”  
”The Dove”(1915) depicts the creation process. It draws upon Christian symbols such as the dove for spirit, peace and unity. It also thematizes the battle between the forces of light and darkness through the allegory of Saint George and the Dragon.
The series ”The Dove” are displayed in the Upstairs Galleries.
Watch our curator of learning Susanne Lindblad present one of the works from the series ”The Dove”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Altarpieces+
**Hilma af Klint, Altarpiece, No. 1, 1915 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet**
Hilma af Klint understood the three powerful ”Altarpieces”(1915) as the essence of ”The Paintings for the Temple”. These works capture the two directions of spiritual evolution: the ascension from the material world back to unity (the triangle pointing to the golden circle) and the descension from divine unity into the diversity of the material world (the inverted triangle). In the third and final painting, a small six-pointed star within the large golden circle is an esoteric symbol for the universe.
”Altarpieces” are displayed in the Upstairs Galleries.
Watch our curator of learning Susanne Lindblad present ”Altarpieces”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Researcher+
Hilma af Klint, Group 2, No title, No. 14a–No. 21, 1919 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
New Gallery is dedicated to Hilma af Klint the researcher, specifically her effort to process and understand the deeper meaning of her spiritually guided work in paintings, drawings and writing, from the 1890s to 1930s. Af Klint had an inquisitive mind. She came from a family of naval officers and nautical cartographers and approached her artistic practice with structured rigor. While she had the courage to open herself to let something larger flow through her while painting, she approached the resulting body of work in a systematic and analytic way.
Throughout her life, af Klint took copious notes, regarding her experiences and interpretations of the messages she apprehended through her spiritual practice. After completing “The Paintings for the Temple”, the artist tried to methodically gain an overview of her work and its possible meanings. In the spirit of a scientific researcher, she edited and reorganized her early notes, created a dictionary of the symbols that appeared in her works and catalogued all the works in “The Paintings for the Temple”in a portable portfolio. Remarkably, af Klint understood all of her works of art as a unified project – a notion radical for the time, but also a testament to the fact that she believed her work to have a higher purpose.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin
texts.4:
# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.
texts.5:
# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.
texts.6:
# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

# In-depth Hilma af Klint
10.4 2015
Hilma af Klint (1862–1944) was a pioneer of abstraction. As early as 1906 she had developed a rich, symbolic imagery that preceded the more broadly recognized emergence of abstract art. Since her retrospective at Moderna Museet in Stockholm in 2013, interest in the Swedish artist has increased all over the world. The exhibition "Hilma af Klint – Artist, Researcher, Medium"further expands our understanding of this groundbreaking artist and researcher.
Hilma af Klint, The Swan, No. 17, 1915 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
Hilma af Klint studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 where she focused on naturalistic landscape and portrait paintings. Like many of her contemporaries, af Klint also had a keen interest in invisible dimensions that exist beyond the visible world. When painting she was convinced that she was in contact with higher consciousness, which conveyed messages through her. Her major series, “The Paintings for the Temple”, became the crux of this artistic inquiry.
The exhibition centres on three aspects of Hilma af Klint’s life and interests – as artist, researcher and medium – that are key to revealing and understanding her art. With few exceptions, af Klint never exhibited her abstract works during her lifetime. Yet she left us with a radical body of work – unprecedented in its use of color, scale and composition – which she hoped future audiences might be better able to sense and decode.
Hilma af Klint made paintings for the future, and that future is now.
texts.3:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Artist and medium
Like many of her contemporaries at the turn of the twentieth century, Hilma af Klint sought to expand her consciousness in order to gain a wider perspective on what we perceive as reality. Consciousness remains one of the deepest mysteries in our time, a subject eagerly explored in neurology, psychology, quantum physics and epigenetics. As part of her spiritual practice, af Klint meditated, adhered to a vegetarian diet, and studied Theosophy and Rosicrucianism. These two esoteric schools thought knowledge of a deeper spiritual reality could be achieved through focused attention on intuition, meditation, and other means of transcending normal human consciousness. Over a period of ten years, af Klint met weekly with four other women, known as De fem (“The Five”). They trained their capability to access or “channel” higher levels of consciousness through contact with spiritual guides known as De Höga(“The Masters”). Af Klint received a specific assignment, which she accepted, known as “The Paintings for the Temple”. She worked throughout her life to understand the deeper meaning embedded in these works.
> “The pictures were painted directly through me, without any preliminary drawings and with great force. I had no idea what the paintings were supposed to depict; nevertheless, I worked swiftly and surely, without changing a single brushstroke
The artist described how she painted the series as a medium, where shapes, colors and compositions came to her. Although af Klint perceived these works as flowing uninhibitedly through her guided hand, she very much applied herself and all her skills in the process: she worked methodically and sequentially in series, divided into thematically and formally focused groups exploring different aspects of cosmic and human evolution.
texts.4:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## The paintings for the temple
Between 1906 and 1915, Hilma af Klint created “The Paintings for the Temple”. It comprises 193 paintings and drawings, divided into series and groups. Works produced between 1906 and 1908 are on view in the Turbine Hall; works from the second part of the series from 1912 to 1915 are on view in the upstairs galleries at Moderna Museet Malmö.
The overall theme of the series is to convey different aspects of human evolution, instigated by polarity. ”The Paintings for the Temple” also thematizes different stages of development that every human being goes through during life on earth. The temple in the title refers not only to a physical building, which af Klint imagined would house the work, but also to the body as a temple for the soul.
texts.5:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Eros and The Seven-pointed Star+
Hilma af Klint, The Eros Series, No. 8, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
The exhibition opens with the joyful series dedicated to Eros, the Greek god of love, associated with fertility and desire. Full of life, these pink-hued works take up the theme of polarity between male and female as the driving force of evolution. These abstract works completely differ from the classic representation of Eros.
In the series “The Seven-Pointed Star”(1908), Hilma af Klint experimented with a greater economy of line, depicting spiraling energy expanding outwards and forming new centres. As is the case with most of af Klint’s work, there is no singular meaning. Seven is a sacred number in many cultures, associated with divine order, and also the eternal harmony of the universe. In Theosophy the star cluster, known as the Seven Stars or the Pleiades, transmits spiritual energy that eventually reaches the human plane.
The series ”Eros” and ”The Seven-pointed Star” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our art educator Ellen Arvidsson present one of the works from the series ”Eros”
texts.6:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Ten Largest+
Hilma af Klint, De tio största, nr 3, Ynglingaåldern, grupp IV, 1907 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk. Photo: Albin Dahlström / Moderna Museet
Like many of the other series within “The Paintings for the Temple”, “The Ten Largest”seems somehow unfettered by limitations of place and time. Across ten canvases, swirling shapes in soft pastel colors rhythmically interact with cursive letters, forming a kind of visual poem. Petals, ovaries, flowers and spirals pulsate in constant sparks of creation. Hilma af Klint attributed this series to the exploration of the human life cycle, from childhood and youth to adulthood and old age. The artist created the ten works between November and December of 1907 on large sheets of paper later glued onto canvas. Given the unusual scale of the works, it is likely that af Klint painted each canvas, while it was lying flat on her studio floor.
The series ”The Ten Largest” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our art educator Mimmi Sjöö present one of the works from the series ”The Ten Largest”
texts.7:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### Primordial Chaos+
Hlma af Klint, Primordial Chaos, No. 15, 1906 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
”Primordial Chaos” (1906–07) is devoted to the creation of the physical world. From the original unity a polarized world arose out of spirit, shown here as feminine (blue and the eyelet) and masculine (yellow and the hook), and also as W (material) and U (spirit). These works are full of spirals of energy and sparks of creation, of symbols of fertility and rebirth (sperm, snakes, crosses).
”Primorial Chaos” is displayed in the Turbine hall.
texts.8:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Evolution+
Hilma af Klint, The Evolution, No. 7, 1908 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
The theme of the evolution of consciousness runs throughout “The Paintings for the Temple”. In the series ”Evolution” (1908), the process of development is shown through the interplay between polarities: male and female, light and darkness, good and evil. Compositionally these works strive to find a balance, in horizontal and vertical mirroring. Hilma af Klint’s exploration seems aligned with the theosophist notion of evolution as a spiritual process, extending beyond the biological perspective on human development that, with the publishing of Darwin’s ”The Evolution of the Species” fifty years earlier, had gained widespread notoriety. This series ends the first part of “The Paintings for the Temple”, as the commission was paused between 1908 and 1912.
The series ”Evololution” are displayed in the Turbine hall.
Watch our curator of learning Susanne Lindblad present one of the works from the series ”Evolution”
texts.9:
# In-depth Hilma af Klint
## Series and groups
### The Swan and The Dove+
Hilma af Klint, The Dove, No. 1, 1915 © Stiftelsen Hilma af Klints Verk Photo: Albin Dahlström/Moderna Museet
When Hilma af Klint resumed her work on ”The Paintings for the Temple” in 1912, her abstraction became more geometric in nature, and Christian symbols became increasingly pronounced. When working, the artist was still in contact with higher planes of consciousness but was encouraged to interpret spiritual messages more freely.
Viewed in sequence, ”The Swan”(1914–15) has a distinct visual rhythm. Often a horizontal line breaks the canvases into two sections where opposite forces meet – light and dark, male and female, life and death. These poles unfold as a black and white swan. Eventually, figuration gives way to abstraction in a fuller spectrum of color. In the final work in the series, the swan pair returns, unified at the centre, intertwined yet distinct and balanced as male and female poles.
The series ”The Swan” are displayed in the Upstairs Galleries.
Watch our art educator Sannie Johansen present one of the works from the series ”The Swan”  
”The Dove”(1915) depicts the creation process. It draws upon Christian symbols such as the dove for spirit, peace and unity. It also thematizes the battle between the forces of light and darkness through the allegory of Saint George and the Dragon.
The series ”The Dove” are displayed in the Upstairs Galleries.
Watch our curator of learning Susanne Lindblad present one of the works from the series ”The Dove”
